title: Needs, wants and spending psychology
objective: Sort expenses into needs and wants and spot two common spending triggers

sources.name: ASIC Moneysmart: Buy now pay later

q.prompt: Why do online stores show a countdown like **'Sale ends in 02:14:09'**?

options.text: Urgency makes us decide fast, before we think it through
To help shoppers plan their budgets
options.why: It's designed to rush you, not to help you plan.
No law requires countdowns. They're a sales tactic.

q.explanation: Time pressure pushes us to act on impulse. Spotting the tactic gives you back the choice.

q.prompt: Have a go: need or want?
q.explanation: Needs keep you housed, fed, healthy and able to work. Wants make life nicer but you could skip them.

screens.title: Needs vs wants
screens.body: A **need** keeps you housed, fed, safe and able to work. A **want** makes life better but is optional. Many things are both: you need transport, but a new car over a used one is a want. The need is the basic version; the upgrade is the want.

screens.title: Four common spending triggers
screens.body: **Urgency**: 'only 2 left', countdowns. **Social**: scrolling, influencers, keeping up with friends. **Feelings**: stress, boredom, payday 'treat yourself'. **Easy payment**: tap-and-go or [[buy now pay later]] makes spending feel painless. Name the trigger, then pause.

visual.name: Brain
visual.caption: Most impulse buys start with a trigger, not a plan

screens.title: What Liam learns
screens.body: Seeing the split shows him where choice really lives.

lines: Most takeaway was after late shifts: a **feelings** trigger he can plan for

q.prompt: Match each moment to its trigger.
pairs: Online shopping after a bad day
q.hint: Ask what's pushing you: the clock, other people, or your mood?
q.explanation: Low stock rushes you (urgency), others' lives prompt comparison (social), and mood-driven buys are feelings.

q.prompt: Mei spent $320 on takeaway, $90 on a phone plan, $60 on games and $410 on groceries. How much went on **wants**?
q.hint: The phone plan and groceries are needs. Add the other two.

q.prompt: A mobile phone is always a want.
q.hint: Think about the basic version versus the upgrade.
q.explanation: A basic phone is a need for most people (work, banking, safety). The latest model is the want.

q.sentence: Waiting 24 hours before buying something unplanned gives the ___ time to fade.
q.explanation: Most urges fade with time. A short pause lets you decide with a clear head.

q.prompt: Liam cuts takeaway from $260 to $160 a month by cooking after late shifts. How much does he keep in a year?
q.explanation: $100 a month × 12 = $1,200 a year from one planned change.

q.prompt: Payday hits and Sara buys $180 of clothes she hadn't planned, thinking 'I've earned it'. Which trigger is this?

options.why: Nothing was rushing her. The push came from her mood about payday.
No one else was involved. It was her own 'treat yourself' feeling.

q.explanation: 'I've earned it' on payday is an emotional trigger. Planning a small, budgeted treat beats an unplanned splurge.

q.prompt: You see headphones you love at 40% off, ending tonight. They weren't in your plan. What's the best first move?

options.text: Pause, check your budget, and buy only if it still fits
Buy now: 40% off is too good to miss
options.why: A discount on something you didn't plan to buy is still extra spending.

options.text: Buy with buy now pay later so it doesn't hurt today
options.why: That hides the cost; it doesn't remove it.

q.explanation: A sale saves money only if you'd have bought it anyway. Pause and check first.

screens.title: Spot your trigger
screens.body: Think of your last purchase you regretted. What pushed you: urgency, social, feelings or easy payment? Knowing your main trigger is the first defence.
screens.action: Name your most common **spending trigger** and one way to pause next time.

bullets: Needs keep you housed, fed and working; wants are optional upgrades.
Common triggers: urgency, social, feelings and easy payment.
A short pause before unplanned buys lets the urge fade.

reviewBank.explanation: Rego and medicine are essentials. Brunch out and spare sneakers are nice-to-haves.

reviewBank.prompt: A one-tap 'Pay in 4' button at checkout mainly works through which trigger?

options.why: It isn't about time running out.

reviewBank.explanation: Splitting a price into small parts makes spending feel painless, so it's an easy-payment trigger.

reviewBank.prompt: Buying something on sale always saves you money.
reviewBank.explanation: It only saves money if you'd have bought it anyway. Otherwise it's spending you didn't plan.
